strengths: Comprehensive, well-engineered end-to-end pipeline covering automated tool-augmented SFT data synthesis, agentic RL with GRPO/DAPO-style optimization, and a scalable asynchronous training infrastructure (request-level scheduling, partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing).

Strong empirical results: AgentMath variants outperform many open-source tool-augmented and text-only baselines of comparable scale on AIME24/25 and HMMT25, and the 30B-A3B MoE model is competitive with much larger dense/MoE models.

Extensive ablation studies (Table 2, 3, 5, Figures 3-7) quantitatively isolate the contributions of tool-augmented data vs text-only data, multi-stage RL, and data refinement/scaling, giving reasonably convincing evidence for design choices.

Systems contributions are concretely measured, with reported 4-5x throughput improvement and detailed breakdown of speedup sources (Table 6, 7), which could be useful engineering knowledge for the community.
Case studies illustrate emergent code self-correction behavior, adding qualitative support to claims about agentic tool-use learning.
weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow, restricted to three math competition benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25); no broader math benchmarks (e.g., MATH, OlympiadBench) or out-of-domain/general reasoning tasks are used to assess generality of the approach or check for overfitting to competition-style tool use.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (code-injection SFT data synthesis, GRPO/DAPO-based agentic RL, asynchronous/partial rollout systems) closely resemble or extend existing works (ReTool, ToRL, START, CoRT, AReaL, rStar2-Agent) already discussed in related work; the main contribution appears to be careful combination/engineering rather than a fundamentally new method.

There is an internal inconsistency between the HMMT25 accuracy reported in the abstract/Table 1 (73.8%) and the number stated in the Conclusion (78.9%), raising concerns about carefulness of reporting.

The largest model (235B-A22B) is trained only via SFT without RL due to compute constraints, undermining the claim that the full AgentMath pipeline (including RL) scales to the largest models, and making the reported SOTA numbers at that scale less representative of the complete method.

Potential data contamination/leakage risks are only partially addressed through n-gram/MinHash/embedding-similarity filtering; given the well-known nature of these competition benchmarks and the use of teacher models on public data pools, residual contamination cannot be fully ruled out.
Key reward hyperparameters (α, β, Rmax in the tool-usage reward) are never explicitly specified, limiting reproducibility of the RL reward design.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported despite using avg@32, and no compute-matched comparisons against other agentic RL tool-use baselines are provided, making it hard to assess whether gains stem from the proposed techniques or simply larger training budgets/data scale.

The paper is very long with substantial content deferred to the appendix, and some core methodological details (e.g., exact segment lengths, full agentic loop pseudocode integration with GRPO) require piecing together information across many sections.

strengths: Comprehensive end-to-end system spanning data synthesis, RL algorithm design, and training infrastructure, with results reported across a wide range of model scales (1.7B to 235B).
Strong reported accuracy numbers on AIME24/25 and HMMT25 relative to many open-source baselines of comparable size, including MoE variants.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (Table 2, 3, 5) isolating the contribution of tool-augmented SFT data vs. text-only data, and of each data-refinement stage.

The systems contributions (request-level asynchronous rollout, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing) are concretely quantified with measured speedups (4-5x), which is useful for practitioners building similar agentic RL pipelines.
Detailed appendix with prompts, algorithm pseudocode, and additional ablations (partial rollout segment count, data scaling law) that aid understanding of design choices.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental: the SFT data-synthesis pipeline (code injection + refinement), GRPO/DAPO-style agentic RL with output masking, and asynchronous rollout infrastructure closely resemble techniques already present in cited prior work (ReTool, ToRL, CoRT, START, DAPO, AReaL, SimpleTIR); the paper's contribution reads primarily as a careful, large-scale engineering combination rather than a new algorithmic or conceptual advance.

Evaluation is confined almost entirely to AIME/HMMT-style competition mathematics; there is no evaluation on broader math benchmarks (e.g., MATH, GSM8K, Olympiad-Bench) or non-math reasoning/tool-use tasks, limiting evidence of generalization beyond a narrow, potentially saturating benchmark family.

There is a numeric inconsistency between the abstract/main results table (HMMT25 = 73.8% for AgentMath-30B-A3B) and the conclusion section, which states 78.9% for the same model/benchmark — this kind of inconsistency raises concerns about the overall rigor and proofreading of empirical claims.

Comparisons across baselines in Table 1/4 mix different base models (Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-Distill, Qwen3) and training paradigms, making some head-to-head comparisons only loosely controlled; base-model differences likely confound part of the reported gains.
Key reward hyperparameters (α, β, R_max in the tool-usage reward) are never given numerical values anywhere in the main text or appendix, hindering reproducibility of the RL reward design.

The flagship 235B model is trained via SFT only (no RL), which weakens the paper's central narrative that agentic RL is essential for unlocking strong tool-use behavior, since the SFT-only model still performs competitively with RL-trained smaller models.

Emergent self-correction and 'code refinement' capabilities are supported primarily by a single anecdotal case study rather than any systematic quantitative analysis of error-recovery rates or self-correction success frequency.
No variance/error bars are reported despite using avg@32, and no statistical significance testing is provided for the reported gains over baselines.

The data-synthesis and quality-control pipeline depends heavily on proprietary or large teacher models (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-32B verifier) for generation and judgment, which increases replication cost/difficulty for other researchers and is not discussed as a limitation.

Multi-stage RL length/tool-call thresholds (48k→72k→96k, 48→72→96 calls) appear to be manually tuned heuristics without ablation of alternative schedules, raising questions about generality to other domains or model families.

strengths: Strong empirical results: AgentMath achieves SOTA or near-SOTA performance on AIME24/25 and HMMT25 across multiple model scales (1.7B to 235B), often outperforming much larger dense/pure-text models and even approaching flagship proprietary systems.

Thorough ablation studies quantifying the contribution of each component: Table 3 isolates the effect of each data-refinement stage, Table 2/Fig 4 compare tool-augmented vs. text-only SFT/RL, and Fig 7 studies data-scaling laws for the synthesis pipeline.

The infrastructure contributions (request-level asynchronous rollout scheduling, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing) are practically useful and are supported by concrete efficiency measurements (4-5x speedup, Table 6, Table 7), which is valuable for the broader RL-for-agents community independent of the math application.

The automated data synthesis pipeline (code injection + multi-stage verification + self-correction injection) is a reasonable and scalable alternative to costly manual annotation (e.g., CoRT) or noisy prompt-only generation (e.g., START), and its necessity is empirically justified.
Extensive appendix with detailed prompts, algorithm pseudocode, training/evaluation settings, and case studies that aid reproducibility and understanding of the emergent self-correction behavior.
Multi-stage RL curriculum (progressively expanding context length and tool-call budget) is well-motivated by empirical truncation statistics and clearly shown to improve accuracy at each stage.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: most individual components (code-injection data synthesis, GRPO/DAPO-based agentic RL with tool masking, partial rollout for long-tail mitigation, async serving) closely resemble existing techniques (ReTool, START, CoRT, ToRL, AReaL, DAPO); the paper's contribution is largely a systems-level integration/engineering effort rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Evaluation is narrowly restricted to three competition-style math benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25); no results on broader math suites (MATH, GSM8K, OlympiadBench) or general/non-math reasoning tasks, making it hard to assess generalization of the approach.

There is an unresolved numerical inconsistency between the abstract/Table 1 (HMMT25 = 73.8%) and the Conclusion section, which states AgentMath-30B-A3B achieves "90.6%, 86.4%, and 78.9%" — suggesting insufficient proofreading and raising minor concerns about result reporting accuracy.

The largest model (235B-A22B) is trained only via SFT due to compute constraints, so the paper's central claim about the benefit of agentic RL is not validated at the largest scale, weakening the overall narrative of scalability.

The data synthesis pipeline depends heavily on a strong proprietary-adjacent teacher model (DeepSeek-V3) and multiple auxiliary verifier models (Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-30B), which increases cost and complexity and may hinder exact reproducibility for groups without similar resources.

No ablation isolating the individual contribution of the reward components (Racc vs. Rtool), so it's unclear how sensitive results are to the tool-usage reward design, or whether it could incentivize superfluous tool calls.

Claims of "emergent" code self-correction capability are illustrated with only two qualitative case studies rather than a systematic quantitative analysis (e.g., frequency/success rate of self-correction events across the test set).

No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing reported for avg@32 accuracy numbers, despite fine-grained differences (e.g., <1%) being used to argue superiority over baselines.

strengths: Comprehensive end-to-end system spanning data synthesis, agentic RL, and training infrastructure, with each component individually ablated (e.g., Table 3 progressive refinement, Table 6/7 infrastructure speedups, Table 27 reward design ablation).

Strong empirical results across a wide range of model scales (1.7B to 235B parameters) on AIME24/25 and HMMT25, with AgentMath-30B-A3B outperforming several larger dense/proprietary models and being competitive with o3/Gemini-2.5-Pro.

Extensive and serious effort to address data contamination concerns via a late-2025 benchmark (Google-IMO-AnswerBench), evaluation with base models pretrained before benchmark release, and a 3-stage deduplication pipeline (exact match, n-gram+MinHash LSH, semantic embedding).

Concrete and reproducible engineering contributions for scaling agentic RL to ultra-long sequences with heavy tool use (request-level async scheduling, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing), yielding a documented 4-5x throughput improvement.

Reasonably transparent methodology: prompts, algorithms, and hyperparameters are provided in detail, and a fair, controlled comparison against ReTool under matched settings is included to isolate the contribution of the proposed data-synthesis method from teacher-model effects.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core techniques (GRPO/DAPO-style RL, code-interleaved reasoning with <think>/<code>/<interpreter> tags, masking interpreter tokens, partial rollout for long-tail mitigation) are incremental combinations of ideas already present in ReTool, ToRL, SimpleTIR, and prior async RL infra work (RollFlash, AReaL, etc.), which are not sufficiently differentiated.

Heavy reliance on distillation from strong teacher models (DeepSeek-R1/V3, Qwen3-30B as judge) raises questions about how much of the improvement stems from the proposed pipeline versus simply inheriting more/better teacher-generated content; the controlled comparisons only partially disentangle this (e.g., AM-Thinking comparison still shows a 4% gap attributable to method, which is real but modest relative to the paper's central claims).

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers across sections (e.g., HMMT25 accuracy for AgentMath-30B-A3B is 73.8% in the abstract/tables but 74.3%/78.9% in other places in the text), which undermines confidence in the reported results and suggests insufficient proofreading.

The extremely long appendix (Sections A.10–A.16) reads as a post-hoc rebuttal addressing likely reviewer concerns (contamination, fairness vs. teacher distillation, reward design justification), suggesting these issues were not adequately resolved in the main submission and were added reactively rather than being part of a principled original design.

Human evaluation of code-complexity filtering relies on only 3 annotators over 280 samples, and several claims about data quality (e.g., 84% of code substitutions being 'reasonable') rely on small-scale, potentially subjective manual annotation without inter-annotator agreement statistics.

Comparisons to some of the strongest, most recent open tool-integrated RL agents (e.g., rStar2-Agent-32B, SimpleTIR) are present in tables but not deeply analyzed or discussed relative to AgentMath's specific advantages, and evaluation is narrowly focused on AIME/HMMT-style competition math, limiting evidence of broader generalization (the GPQA and IMO-AnswerBench extensions are relatively brief and less rigorously ablated than the main math results).

strengths: Extensive experimental scope across model scales (1.7B to 235B parameters), with SFT and RL results reported for several backbones.
Reasonably strong empirical results on AIME24/25 and HMMT25, with AgentMath-30B-A3B showing competitive numbers versus larger open and some proprietary models.

System-engineering contributions (request-level async rollout scheduling, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing) that report a 4-5x throughput improvement for long-sequence, tool-heavy RL training, which is a useful practical engineering result.
Fairly detailed ablations on the data-refinement pipeline (format correction, executability verification, self-correction injection) and on scaling of synthetic data volume.
Reproducibility statement and inclusion of prompts used for data synthesis and judging.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core recipe (tool-augmented CoT->code trajectory synthesis + GRPO/DAPO-style RL with masked interpreter tokens + partial/async rollout scheduling) is a fairly direct combination of ideas already present in ReTool, ToRL, CoRT, DAPO, and existing asynchronous agentic-RL systems (e.g., AReaL, RollPacker-style approaches); the paper largely repackages known techniques rather than introducing a fundamentally new method.

Heavy reliance on distillation from DeepSeek-R1/V3 as teacher models for SFT data; while the authors attempt to control for this via a matched comparison with ReTool and AM-Thinking, the overall performance gains still appear closely tied to the quality of upstream teacher generations rather than a clearly separable methodological contribution.

Evaluation is dominated by very small benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25 each have ~30 problems), which are well-known to be susceptible to memorization/contamination; the paper's own extensive appendix devoted to defending benchmark reliability (IMO-AnswerBench, pre-2025 base models, etc.) suggests this is a substantive, not merely cosmetic, concern that undermines confidence in the main-text SOTA claims.

The comparison table in the main results mixes many different base models, training recipes, and tool-use settings across baselines, making apples-to-apples comparison difficult; claimed 'state-of-the-art' status is often really 'competitive with' or 'approaching' larger/stronger models rather than clearly superior.

The appendix is unusually bloated and appears to contain material that reads like point-by-point rebuttal responses inserted post hoc (e.g., A.10 'Motivation and Core Contributions' essentially restates the introduction; A.11-A.16 contain extensive redundant tables re-deriving results already shown in the main paper), which suggests the submission may not represent a well-organized, originally-conceived paper and raises concerns about the presentation quality expected at a top venue.

Ablation studies (e.g., reward design in A.16, partial rollout segment count) report differences of only 1-2 accuracy points on small benchmarks without variance/significance analysis, making it hard to assess whether the specific design choices are actually load-bearing.
Case studies presented (Appendix A.8) are cherry-picked single examples rather than systematic analysis of the claimed 'emergent self-correction' capability.

The efficiency claims (4-5x speedup) are not benchmarked against other published asynchronous/partial-rollout agentic RL systems under matched hardware/settings, limiting the ability to judge the actual systems contribution relative to prior art.
Overall the paper reads more as a strong applied/systems engineering report than a paper with a clear, novel scientific contribution appropriate for a top-tier research venue.

strengths: Extensive multi-scale empirical validation (1.7B to 235B parameters) with consistent, substantial gains over comparable open-source baselines on AIME24/25 and HMMT25, and competitive results against several proprietary models.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component: data refinement stages, tool-augmented vs. text-only data, multi-stage RL curriculum, segment length choice for data synthesis, code-complexity filtering, and reward design.

Careful and unusually extensive effort to rule out data contamination concerns, including evaluation on a newer benchmark (Google IMO-AnswerBench, released after Qwen3 pretraining cutoff), controlled experiments using base models predating benchmark releases, and a documented multi-stage deduplication pipeline.

Controlled, apples-to-apples comparison against ReTool (same 2k data, same teacher, same base model, same RL steps) isolating the contribution of the proposed data-synthesis method from confounds like base model or teacher choice.

Concrete, quantified systems contributions (request-level async scheduling, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing) yielding a well-documented 4-5x training throughput improvement, which is a genuinely useful engineering contribution given the cost of ultra-long-sequence agentic RL.
Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: detailed prompts, hyperparameters, data construction pipeline, and an explicit reproducibility statement.
Demonstrated generalization beyond math to GPQA (physics/chemistry/biology), suggesting the tool-augmented synthesis pipeline is not narrowly overfit to the competition-math setting.
weaknesses: Core methodological novelty is limited: the RL algorithm is essentially GRPO + DAPO tricks already established in prior literature, and the async/partial-rollout infrastructure ideas closely resemble concurrent systems work (e.g., AReaL, ROLL Flash, RollPacker, all cited by the paper itself); the primary contribution is largely an engineering integration and scaling exercise rather than a new algorithmic idea.

There is a numerical inconsistency between the abstract/main results table (HMMT25 = 73.8%) and the conclusion section, which states 78.9% for the same AgentMath-30B-A3B model, raising minor concerns about carefulness in reporting.

Heavy reliance on distillation from strong teacher models (DeepSeek-R1/V3, Qwen3-30B judge) means much of the absolute performance ceiling is inherited from these teachers; while the ReTool comparison partially controls for this, broader 'state-of-the-art' claims partly reflect teacher quality rather than a fundamentally better learning algorithm.

The reward design (bonus for tool invocation count conditioned on correctness) risks incentivizing superficial tool-call inflation; the provided ablation is fairly narrow (only 100 RL steps, single backbone) and doesn't fully explore failure modes such as gaming behavior over longer training horizons.

The largest model (235B-A22B) is trained only with SFT, not RL, which limits the completeness of the largest-scale results and leaves open whether the RL gains observed at smaller scales would transfer.
Self-correction capability claims are largely illustrated via qualitative case studies rather than a dedicated quantitative benchmark that isolates and measures self-correction ability directly.

The main comparison table aggregates many baselines trained with very different recipes, data, and compute budgets, making some 'state-of-the-art' claims difficult to interpret as strictly controlled comparisons.

The paper is exceptionally long with a ~50-page appendix; while thorough, this raises questions about whether the core contribution is self-contained enough for the main paper, and some appendix material largely restates the main text rather than adding new content.
